Jacob Grimm and Wilhelm Grimm were two German brothers whose collection and curation of European fairy tales became the canonical foundation for the Western fairy-tale tradition. Their Kinder- und Hausmärchen, or Children's and Household Tales, first published in eighteen twelve, transformed oral folktales into a standardized, curated collection that shaped literature, theater, ballet, and music for centuries. The Brothers Grimm demonstrated that folk narratives were worthy of serious scholarly and artistic attention.

They were born in Hanau, Germany in the wake of Enlightenment intellectual ferment. Jacob studied law but shifted toward philology and folklore, while Wilhelm followed a similar path. They collected tales from peasants, friends, and other oral sources across the Harz region and beyond. Their work was not pure folklore studies but rather curated literary texts.

When they first published Kinder- und Hausmärchen in eighteen twelve, the collection contained just eighty-six tales. Over their lifetimes, through multiple editions and translations, the collection grew to over two hundred stories. Each new edition was revised to make the stories more literary and proper, softening violence, adding morals, and Germanizing names. This practice shaped how fairy tales were received and understood across Europe.

The collection included now-iconic tales like Hansel and Gretel, Snow White, Cinderella, Rapunzel, Little Red Riding Hood, Sleeping Beauty, and Rumpelstiltskin. Jacob was the primary linguist and academic scholar, while Wilhelm was the more empathetic editor and storyteller. Their partnership balanced intellectual rigor with narrative grace.

Their influence was immense. They influenced virtually every later fairy-tale adaptation, from ballet libretti to musical theater. This was because their standardized texts became the reference versions taught in schools.

They codified fairy tales as a literary category worthy of serious study. Sondheim's musical Into the Woods directly deconstructs the Grimm-collected canon as its foundational source material. The composer Stephen Sondheim would later critique fairy-tale logic through musical theatre. Their Little Briar Rose became the libretto source for Petipa and Tchaikovsky's ballet, The Sleeping Beauty. The Brothers Grimm exemplified early Romantic interest in folk tradition and cultural nationalism, helping to establish what counts as fairy-tale literature itself.
